title: The Language That Dreams of Thinking

panels.prompt: Dartmouth College seminar room in summer 1956, a small group of men in short-sleeved white shirts sitting casually around a large wooden table, papers and coffee cups scattered everywhere, ashtrays with cigarette smoke curling upward, a green chalkboard behind them reads DARTMOUTH SUMMER RESEARCH PROJECT ON ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE in chalk, the mood is electric and informal, sunlight streaming through tall windows casting warm rectangles on the floor, ivy-covered brick visible through the windows, comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, green #38A169 accent on the chalkboard text

panels.text: In the summer of 1956, a young mathematics professor named John McCarthy organized a now-legendary workshop at Dartmouth College. He invited some of the brightest minds — including Marvin Minsky and Claude Shannon — to spend the summer thinking about one question: Can machines be made to think?

A white speech bubble with black outline near the top right. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Could a computer actually think?" panels.text: In 1958, McCarthy unveiled LISP (LISt Processing). It was unlike anything before. Where FORTRAN dealt with numbers and COBOL with business records, LISP dealt with symbols and lists. It could manipulate code as data. It introduced recursive functions, garbage collection, and dynamic typing — concepts that didn't become mainstream until the 2000s.

panels.caption: LISP was directly inspired by Church's lambda calculus

panels.text: LISP was the first language designed not for calculation or business, but for reasoning. It treated code as data and drew directly from Church's lambda calculus. LISP proved that programming languages could be built not just for what computers do well, but for what we want computers to learn to do.
The pioneers were reshaping what computers could do. But who got to learn these languages? In the early 1960s, one woman fought to make sure the answer was "everyone."
